Where it began

Mohammad Amir was born in Changa Bangial, near Gujar Khan in Punjab, on 13 April 1992, and grew up the second youngest in a family of six boys and a girl. His hero was Wasim Akram. He would watch him on television, then run outside and try to copy every movement of that left arm.

At 11 he caught the eye at a local tournament and was taken into Asif Bajwa's academy in Rawalpindi. Four years later the boy who had copied Wasim Akram was picked out by the man himself at a fast-bowling camp. In his first domestic season, for Rawalpindi Rams and National Bank, he took 55 first-class wickets.

The player

He arrived on the world stage at the 2009 World Twenty20, aged 17. In the final against Sri Lanka he bowled a wicket maiden to open the match, removing Tillakaratne Dilshan, the tournament's leading scorer, and Pakistan went on to lift the trophy.

His Test career began soon afterwards in Sri Lanka, with Kumar Sangakkara out to him in both innings. In July 2010 his seven wickets helped Pakistan beat Australia in a Test for the first time in 15 years, and in England that summer he became the youngest bowler to take five in an innings there and the youngest to reach 50 Test wickets. In all he played 36 Tests between 2009 and 2019, taking 119 wickets at 30.48 with four five-wicket hauls and a best of six for 44.

What made him special

He was quick, often above 145 km/h, and he touched 152 in that first World Twenty20 final. He swung the ball, and his skiddy bouncer hurried batters into mistimed shots.

His finest hour came in the 2017 Champions Trophy final. He removed India's top three: Rohit Sharma leg before for nought, Virat Kohli caught at point after surviving a chance at slip, and Shikhar Dhawan caught behind. He finished with three for 16 from six overs, India were all out for 158 and Pakistan won by 180 runs. Kohli later counted him among the toughest bowlers he had faced.

Wasim Akram once said he needed to put on a bit of weight. Coming from his hero, that was advice worth having.

Away from the middle

He was Pakistan's leading wicket-taker at the 2019 World Cup, with 17 in eight games, including his first one-day five-wicket haul, against Australia. He left Test cricket in July 2019, played in the 2024 T20 World Cup, where his seven wickets cost barely ten runs each, and finished with international cricket in December 2024.

And finally

His Test batting average was 13.41, yet he kept turning up in the one-day record books as a batter. His 73 not out against New Zealand in 2009 was then the highest score by a number ten, and in 2016 at Nottingham his 58 made him the first man to hit a one-day fifty from number eleven. Somebody should have told him where tail-enders are meant to stand.
